metadata.title: Exploration of the assessment of clinical decision-making capabilities in Clinical Oncology based on generative large language models.
metadata.journal: European journal of surgical oncology : the journal of the European Society of Surgical Oncology and the British Association of Surgical Oncology

abstract:
BACKGROUND
With advancements in large language model (LLM) technology, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has shown transformative potential in healthcare, particularly in optimizing clinical workflows through data integration and semantic reasoning for clinical decision support (CDS). However, existing AI models primarily rely on logical deductions from standardized guidelines, and their effectiveness in complex, high-risk clinical scenarios remains to be further validated. This study evaluates the CDS efficacy of DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 in real-world oncology diagnosis and treatment settings, assessing the accuracy and adaptability of their recommendations through a multidimensional framework.


METHODS
A time-sequenced, chain-structured clinical question set was developed based on real oncology cases. Responses from DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 were independently generated and blindly evaluated for accuracy and feasibility by four oncology experts. Statistical analysis and visualization were performed using Prism GraphPad 10.0.


RESULTS
Both DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 demonstrated overall competent performance in oncology CDS, with no significant differences compared to human clinicians. Evaluations using a clinical decision quality assessment scale indicated robust performance for both models. Subgroup analysis revealed that DeepSeek R1 outperformed in medical humanistic care, while ChatGPT-4 o1 excelled in readability. No statistical differences were observed between the two models in knowledge accuracy, test rationality, or medication standardization.


CONCLUSION
Generative AI models such as DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 exhibit comprehensive capabilities in oncology CDS comparable to clinicians, suggesting potential clinical utility. However, AI reliability in complex cases requires improvement and cannot yet replace physicians' expertise. Future research should prioritize multimodal knowledge integration and ethical oversight to enhance AI's role in optimizing diagnostic efficiency and humanistic care quality.

Keywords Oncology  Diagnosis and treatment  Clinical decision support  Large language models  Artificial intelligence   Data availability The data supporting the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Access will be granted for research purposes only, subject to approval by the authors and institutional review boards, to ensure the protection of patient privacy and data security.   1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs), based on the latest advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology, are capable of natural language processing, generation, and understanding through massive data learning and complex semantic reasoning. LLMs use deep learning algorithms to extract knowledge from large amounts of text, possessing powerful semantic understanding and generation capabilities [1 ,2 ]. As a result, they are widely applied in fields such as text generation, machine translation, intelligent question answering, and customer service. In recent years, the application of LLMs in the medical field has also shown significant potential, particularly in optimizing Clinical Decision Support (CDS), where they can integrate medical knowledge, case data, and clinical guidelines to assist doctors in making more precise and efficient clinical decisions [1 ]. Generative large language models, combined with human feedback reinforcement learning, further improve their accuracy and adaptability in clinical decision-making, making them an important direction for future development in the medical field [3 ,4 ]。 However, despite the preliminary application progress of LLMs in some fields, their use in high-risk clinical areas such as oncology remains controversial. Some studies suggest that LLMs can assist doctors in early cancer screening, diagnosis, and treatment decisions by analyzing vast amounts of medical literature and case data, and provide personalized treatment plans for patients [5 ]. For example, studies have shown that large language models such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek can provide reasonable diagnostic suggestions during cancer diagnosis and treatment, performing excellently in some standardized case analyses [6 ,7 ]. However, other studies point out that although existing LLMs can provide treatment recommendations based on standardized guidelines, they still have limitations when faced with dynamic and individualized clinical demands. In particular, when handling complex, high-risk cancer treatment decisions, the reasoning ability of LLMs is still insufficient to replace the judgment of experienced clinical doctors [8 ,9 ]. Therefore, the clinical application of LLMs in oncology still requires further validation and exploration. This study aims to evaluate the clinical decision support effectiveness of DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 in real-world oncology treatment scenarios. By constructing a multidimensional evaluation framework, this study focuses on verifying the accuracy and clinical adaptability of these two generative AI models' treatment recommendations in oncology. The core objective of this study is to explore the practical application value of LLMs in oncology through the evaluation of real-world data, providing scientific evidence for the optimization and practice of large language models in medical decision-making. Through the performance evaluation of these two AI models, this study not only provides a new perspective on the application of medical AI, but also offers theoretical support for advancing the reliability and effectiveness of AI in complex clinical environments.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Problem acquisition and construction The problem construction in this study is based on real clinical records from the oncology center of Nanchong Hospital, affiliated with Capital Medical University Beijing Anzhen Hospital and Nanchong City Central Hospital. The data set was formed through systematic screening and structured processing into a standardized question-answer dataset. All medical records follow medical ethical norms, were approved by the hospital ethics committee, and underwent strict de-identification (including full anonymization of sensitive information such as patient names, ID numbers, and contact details) to ensure patient privacy protection. We selected these six tumor types (nasopharyngeal carcinoma, lung cancer, liver cancer, cervical cancer, gastric cancer, and colorectal cancer) as study cases to encompass common malignant tumors, each with distinct clinical presentations, treatment protocols, and pathological features, thereby ensuring that the artificial intelligence model can effectively perform detection, localization, and staging evaluations across diverse clinical scenarios. In this study, the AI models, DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1, were provided with a broad spectrum of contextual patient data, including basic demographic information, laboratory test results, imaging findings, and clinical notes with comorbidities. This dataset was designed to reflect real-world clinical scenarios and assess the models' ability to integrate and reason through complex medical data in oncology decision-making. The structured question design for medical record information focuses on clinical diagnosis and treatment pathways and revolves around the following six key dimensions: (1) analysis of etiology and risk factors; (2) interpretation of laboratory test results; (3) recognition of imaging report characteristics; (4) disease diagnosis and staging; (5) drug treatment plans (including drug types, dosages, treatment duration, and adverse reaction management); (6) indications for surgery and choice of surgical methods. The questions for each case cover several or all of these six dimensions. Based on the clinical characteristics of each case, the question chain adopts a “sequential progression” construction strategy, simulating the real clinical decision-making process: from history collection and preliminary differential diagnosis to the gradual extension of test selection, treatment plan formulation, and dynamic adjustments. The detailed procedure is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 . The clinical rationality and logical rigor of all questions were double-validated: firstly, the question framework was independently reviewed by two senior oncologists (with ≥10 years of experience) to ensure compliance with both the Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) guidelines and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines [10 ,11 ]. For example, in determining the indications for targeted therapy, both the domestic practice recommendations of CSCO and the international evidence-based standards of NCCN were considered. The differences and similarities between the CSCO and NCCN guidelines were compared, resulting in a standardized question set that balances local clinical applicability and international cutting-edge standards. This process also eliminated open-ended questions that were controversial or lacked sufficient evidence, ensuring the interpretability and comparability of the evaluation results. Finally, based on the collected cases, six main case topics were developed, including 29 chain-type clinical case questions.  2.2 Application of generative large language models in question-answering This study selected the DeepSeek R1 version from DeepSeek, a Chinese company specializing in AI technology research, and the ChatGPT-4 o1 version from OpenAI as representatives of generative large language models. ChatGPT-4 o1 is based on the GPT-4-4 architecture, developed by OpenAI, and is optimized for a broad range of natural language processing tasks. DeepSeek R1 is a general-purpose generative language model developed by DeepSeek, similar in architecture to ChatGPT, but it is designed for various applications, including clinical decision support. Both models use transformer-based architectures, and each was trained on large, diverse datasets, enabling them to handle a wide range of tasks, including clinical decision-making [12 ,13 ]. In April 2025, the authors submitted the 29 chain-type clinical case questions mentioned earlier to the two large language models in clinical diagnosis and treatment sequence. To reduce bias in the model's answers, the study did not use “Custom Instructions” for personalized medical knowledge settings, nor did it use any prompts to limit the large language models to acting as “assistant physicians.” Each chain of questions for the cases was asked independently using the “new chat” feature, and each was repeated three times to obtain stable results.  2.3 Feasibility assessment of generative large language model responses to clinical questions To assess the ability and feasibility of large language models in providing specialized knowledge for the treatment of cancer patients, four experienced oncologists were organized to score the clinical real-case answers from DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1, using the “Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) Treatment Guidelines” and the “National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines” as reference. The evaluation was blind, meaning that the evaluating physicians were unaware of which model provided the answers. The evaluation used a scoring system from 0 to 5, where 0 represents “completely does not meet” and 5 represents “completely meets,” with scores of 3 or above considered passing. The accuracy of the model's answers was quantified, and each model's answer to each question was evaluated three times by professional physicians, with the average score taken as the final result. In addition, based on dual standards from CSCO and NCCN guidelines, we developed a Clinical Decision Quality Assessment Scale (CDQAS) (Supplementary Table 1 ) using a consensus method to evaluate the large language model's capabilities in multiple dimensions. The scale includes six dimensions: readability (Maximum 10 points), medical knowledge accuracy (Maximum 30 points), rationality of tests and examinations (Maximum 20 points), medication standardization (Maximum 20 points), medical humanism (maximum 10 points), logical coherence (Maximum 10 points). The total maximum score for the scale is 100 points. The scale determined the weight of each evaluation dimension through the Delphi expert consultation method. For each corresponding dimension, the model's case analysis answers were independently evaluated by four oncologists, with the average score used as the final score for that dimension. If there were discrepancies between CSCO and NCCN, the clarification of evidence-based medical references and applicable scenarios would serve as a scoring adjustment. The expert panel consisted of four senior oncologists with over 10 years of experience in the field of oncology, ensuring the authority and professionalism of the evaluation. The Delphi method was employed through three rounds of surveys to ensure consensus on the weighting of each dimension. In cases of significant disagreement among experts, discrepancies were resolved through collective discussion and a subsequent round of anonymous voting, ensuring a final consensus was reached.  2.4 Statistical analysis To compare the performance of DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 on each question, we took the average of the corresponding scores to obtain a comprehensive score for each chain-type clinical question. Since the sample size is small and does not follow a normal distribution, the paired Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to assess whether the performance differences between the two models on the same question were statistically significant. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. To assess the difference magnitude, we calculated the Rank-Biserial effect size, based on the Mann-Whitney U  test, to quantify the strength of the difference. Inter-rater consistency was calculated using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient. Additionally, this study performed subgroup analysis based on the 6 dimensions of the CDQAS. All statistical data and analysis results will be visualized using Prism GraphPad 10.0 software.   3 Results 3.1 Overall scoring of clinical real-world cases Four oncologists independently evaluated the responses of DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 for 6 clinical real-world cases, while also assessing the diagnostic and treatment process of real-world clinical physicians. The evaluation results are presented in Table 1  . Statistical analysis revealed that the accuracy and feasibility of DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 are similar, with no statistical difference when compared to the evaluation results of real-world clinical physicians, p > 0.05 (Fig. 1  ).  3.2 Clinical decision quality assessment scale analysis Based on the CDQAS scale, four oncologists individually evaluated the assessment results of DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 for 6 clinical real-world cases. The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) analysis showed that the ICC for the DeepSeek R1 ratings was 0.741, and for the ChatGPT-4 o1 ratings, it was 0.778, indicating good to strong consistency between the raters. The evaluation results are shown in Table 2  . DeepSeek R1 scored an average of 81.83 points, while ChatGPT-4 o1 scored an average of 78.17 points. The two models have comparable capabilities in providing clinical decision quality (Fig. 2  ).  3.3 Subgroup analysis of clinical decision quality assessment scale In terms of readability, the maximum score is 10 points. After evaluation by the physicians, DeepSeek R1 scored 7.33, 6.33, 7.17, 6.67, while ChatGPT-4 o1 scored 8.5, 8.17, 8, 7.5. ChatGPT-4 o1 outperformed DeepSeek R1 in terms of readability in clinical decision-making, with a statistically significant difference (p < 0.05) (Fig. 3  A). The Rank-Biserial effect size of r = 1.165 with a 95 %CI of (0.17, 2.17) supports a substantial difference between the two groups. In terms of medical knowledge accuracy, the maximum score is 30 points. After physician evaluation, DeepSeek R1 scored 26.67, 25.5, 26.19, 25.67, while ChatGPT-4 o1 scored 26, 25.83, 25, 23.83. The difference in the accuracy of clinical decision-making between DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 was not statistically significant (p > 0.05) (Fig. 3 B). In terms of the rationality of tests and examinations, the maximum score is 20 points. After physician evaluation, DeepSeek R1 scored 17.5, 17.17, 15.5, 15, while ChatGPT-4 o1 scored 16.17, 17.33, 15, 14.83. The difference in the rationality of clinical decision-making between DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 was not statistically significant (p > 0.05) (Fig. 3 C). In terms of medication standardization, the maximum score is 20 points. After physician evaluation, DeepSeek R1 scored 18.5, 15.83, 16.3, 16.33, while ChatGPT-4 o1 scored 15.5, 16.5, 17, 16.83. The difference in medication standardization in clinical decision-making between DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 was not statistically significant (p > 0.05) (Fig. 3 D). In terms of medical humanism, the maximum score is 10 points. After physician evaluation, DeepSeek R1 scored 6.83, 7.33, 8.33, 8.83, while ChatGPT-4 o1 scored 4.5, 5.17, 5.33, 5.67. DeepSeek R1 outperformed ChatGPT-4 o1 in medical humanism in clinical decision-making, with a statistically significant difference (p < 0.05) (Fig. 3 E). The Rank-Biserial effect size of r = −2.58 with a 95 %CI of (−4.33, −0.16) supports a substantial difference between the two groups. In terms of logical coherence, the maximum score is 10 points. After physician evaluation, DeepSeek R1 scored 8.33, 7.5, 7.83, 8.33, while ChatGPT-4 o1 scored 8.17, 6.5, 8.17, 7.17. The difference in logical coherence of clinical decision-making between DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 was not statistically significant (p > 0.05) (Fig. 3 F).   4 Discussion This study, through a multidimensional evaluation system, demonstrates that generative large language models have certain application value in clinical disease diagnosis and treatment in the oncology department. The results show that DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 perform similarly in overall clinical decision support, slightly weaker than the real-world clinical physician level, indicating their potential application prospects in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning in the field of oncology. There is no significant difference between DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 in core medical capabilities such as medical knowledge accuracy, rationality of tests and examinations, and medication standardization. However, it is noteworthy that, although the quality of answers generally met the passing standard, in some complex clinical cases (such as nasopharyngeal cancer treatment plans), the answers provided by AI scored lower and lacked sufficient credibility [14 ]. Furthermore, it is important to note that this study did not aim to balance the complexity of the clinical cases. The six cases selected were chosen to represent a range of cancer types and treatment strategies, rather than being a statistically balanced sample. This approach was intended to showcase the diversity of real-world clinical scenarios, but it also means that the complexity of the cases may vary significantly. As such, the findings should be interpreted with caution, as they may not fully reflect the broad spectrum of clinical settings or cancer complexities that might be encountered in a larger, more balanced sample. Therefore, AI should be regarded as an auxiliary tool for physicians in practical applications, and final review by clinical physicians is still required in atypical clinical scenarios [15 ]. DeepSeek R1 significantly outperforms ChatGPT-4 o1 in providing medical humanism, while ChatGPT-4 o1 performs better in clinical decision support readability, suggesting that different AI models may have complementary value in medical settings. By integrating AI systems with both technical precision and medical humanism, it can reduce physician decision-making pressure, and its humanistic features can optimize doctor-patient communication, which is particularly valuable in oncology diagnosis and treatment [16 ,17 ]. In this study, the application of LLMs represented by DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 in CDS demonstrates their potential value, showcasing the advantages of LLMs in semantic understanding, execution of complex diagnostic and treatment tasks, and output of precise treatment plans in clinical settings. In a study on urine cytology for the diagnosis of urothelial carcinoma, an AI model, PUCAS, was developed to improve the sensitivity of urine cytology. In the retrospective cohort, the sensitivity ranged from 0.922 (95 % CI: 0.811–0.978) to 1.000 (95 % CI: 0.782–1.000), and the model reduced unnecessary endoscopies by 57.5 %, with a negative predictive value of 96.4 % [18 ]. Similarly, an AI system based on deep neural networks developed by Peter Ström et al. achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.997 (95 % CI: 0.994–0.999) in distinguishing benign from malignant prostate biopsy cores, with a Gleason grading kappa of 0.62, comparable to expert pathologists [19 ]. Furthermore, in the field of breast cancer diagnosis and care, a study by Deng et al. comparing three large language models (LLMs) showed that GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5 and Claude2 in terms of quality, relevance, and applicability, with significant improvements in four clinical assessment areas, particularly in treatment decision-making and psychosocial support, where GPT-4 scored higher than GPT-3.5 [20 ]. LLMs can reduce decision-making fluctuations caused by human memory biases or limitations of experience by quickly integrating the latest guidelines and evidence-based evidence. Especially in standardized diagnostic and treatment processes, LLM's standardized output based on massive literature may reduce the risks of medication dosage errors or missed tests caused by differences in physicians' clinical experience [21 ]. Research shows that after training with data that includes empathy expression and individualized recommendations, AI models can significantly enhance their ability to provide medical humanism outputs [22 ]. This characteristic makes DeepSeek R1 more adept at generating decision-making suggestions that include prognostic explanations and psychological comfort, aligning with oncology patients' need for emotional support. In terms of readability, ChatGPT-4 o1's excellent performance may be due to its more mature text generation framework, which may be related to reinforcement learning-based dialogue optimization that makes the model's output more structured and logical [23 ]. It is worth noting that future research should focus on how to effectively integrate different LLM technologies to achieve complementary advantages and optimal medical decision support [24 ]. Although the capabilities of LLMs in information processing are impressive, their application in medical decision-making still faces challenges. First, LLMs may lack deep understanding of medical knowledge, which could lead to a risk of reduced decision-making reliability when facing complex or rare cases [25 ]. Secondly, the diagnostic and treatment recommendations from LLMs lack personalization and cannot account for specific patient needs and conditions [25 ]. Therefore, LLMs still need to rely on the professional judgment of physicians when providing clinical decision support [26 ,27 ]. In addition, researchers and developers must strengthen medical ethics review and data privacy protection mechanisms, and establish a safety and compliance framework for LLMs in clinical decision support, ensuring that patient privacy and rights are fully protected [28 ,29 ]. The main limitation of this study is the small sample size, which only covers a subset of common cancer diseases. The conclusions drawn may not have broad statistical inferential significance. Future studies should consider expanding the sample size to validate the generalizability of the current results. Secondly, despite the development of a comprehensive evaluation method, there remains some subjective bias. Future studies should employ validated assessment tools, ensure the reporting of inter-rater reliability, and apply more rigorous analytical frameworks. Furthermore, there is a lag in the knowledge iteration of current AI models, which may result in a lack of timely information [30 ,31 ]. Future research should focus on increasing the sample size and building a more objective evaluation system.  5 Conclusion In conclusion, our study preliminarily shows that the diagnostic accuracy of generative large language models represented by DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 is generally close to that of clinical physicians, demonstrating significant clinical application potential in clinical decision support for cancer diseases. llm_extraction.methods_summary: Time-sequenced, chain-structured clinical question sets (29 questions across 6 real-world cases) were constructed from de-identified oncology records at Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital, covering nasopharyngeal carcinoma, lung cancer, liver cancer, cervical cancer, gastric cancer, and colorectal cancer. Questions spanned six clinical dimensions: etiology/risk factors, laboratory test interpretation, imaging recognition, diagnosis and staging, drug treatment plans, and surgical indications. DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT-4 o1 responded independently using fresh 'new chat' sessions (no custom instructions or persona prompts), each question chain repeated three times. Blind evaluation by four oncologists (≥10 years experience) used two instruments: (1) a 0–5 feasibility scale aligned to CSCO/NCCN guidelines, and (2) a six-dimension Clinical Decision Quality Assessment Scale (CDQAS, max 100 points) developed by three-round Delphi consensus. Average of three evaluations per rater used as final score. Statistical analysis: paired Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Rank-Biserial effect size (Mann-Whitney U), and ICC for inter-rater reliability; visualized in Prism GraphPad 10.0.
llm_extraction.limitations: Very small sample size (6 clinical cases, 29 questions) limits statistical power and generalizability. Cases were selected to represent cancer type diversity rather than difficulty balance, so complexity varied significantly across cases and findings may not reflect the full spectrum of real-world oncology. Novel CDQAS scale was developed specifically for this study and lacks independent external validation. Residual subjective bias exists despite blinding. No custom prompting or clinical persona instructions were applied to models, potentially underestimating their optimized performance. Knowledge lag in AI models may result in outdated treatment recommendations. Study was conducted in a single Chinese institution with CSCO/NCCN-aligned cases, limiting international generalizability. Only two LLMs were compared; no evaluation of other models (Gemini, Claude, etc.). Formal statistical testing of the overall CDQAS score difference between the two models was not explicitly reported.

relationships.description: Builds on Singhal et al. (2023, Nature) showing LLMs encode clinical knowledge, by applying clinical knowledge evaluation to real-world oncology decision-support scenarios with expert blind scoring.
Extends Bedi et al. (2025, JAMA) systematic review on LLM healthcare testing by contributing a domain-specific multidimensional evaluation framework in oncology.
Supports Deng et al. (2024) finding that GPT-4 class models perform well in oncology clinical scenarios, corroborating strong overall performance in cancer decision support.

Supports Lorenzi et al. (2024) finding that LLMs have reliability limitations in complex head and neck malignancy cases; this study similarly observed lower AI scores for complex cases such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Provides empirical support for Moor et al. (2023) vision of foundation models for generalist medical AI by demonstrating competent oncology CDS performance comparable to clinicians.

methodology_details.approach: Comparative evaluation of two generative LLMs (DeepSeek R1, ChatGPT-4 o1) against human clinicians on real-world oncology cases using blind expert scoring with a novel multi-dimensional clinical decision quality scale (CDQAS)
datasets: 6 de-identified real-world oncology cases from Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital (nasopharyngeal carcinoma, lung cancer, liver cancer, cervical cancer, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer)
29 chain-type clinical questions structured across 6 clinical dimensions (etiology, lab interpretation, imaging, diagnosis/staging, drug treatment, surgical indications)
metrics: CDQAS medical knowledge accuracy subscale (max 30 points)
CDQAS rationality of tests and examinations subscale (max 20 points)
Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) for inter-rater reliability
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: Blinded evaluation by 4 oncologists with ≥10 years experience. Each model answered each question chain independently in fresh sessions, repeated 3 times. CDQAS developed by 3-round Delphi consensus. Data available from corresponding author on reasonable request. Analysis performed in Prism GraphPad 10.0.

domain_specific_fields.benchmark: CDQAS (Clinical Decision Quality Assessment Scale) — novel 100-point scale with 6 weighted dimensions, developed by authors using Delphi consensus from CSCO and NCCN guidelines
domain_specific_fields.metrics: CDQAS total and 6 subscores; 0–5 feasibility scale; ICC; Rank-Biserial effect size; paired Wilcoxon rank-sum test p-values
domain_specific_fields.model_architecture: DeepSeek R1 (transformer-based, general-purpose, developed by DeepSeek); ChatGPT-4 o1 (GPT-4 architecture with reinforcement learning-based dialogue optimization, developed by OpenAI)
domain_specific_fields.dataset: 6 real-world oncology cases with 29 chain-type questions from a single Chinese hospital; covers 6 cancer types; evaluated April 2025
